name: Lena Abbott

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI companies, unions or government. This is confidential. Tell me what an ordinary day at the contact centre is like.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m 27 and lead a small call and chat team at the contact centre. I have a two-year college diploma, and I’m one of the agents they send the tangled billing cases to. I live alone and earn on the lower end for this job, even with the team lead duties. My savings are under a month of expenses.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What part of that day stays with you after work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like making the handover notes clear enough that the morning shift can finish a case. The hard bit is listening to the same complaint after a system has already given someone a confident wrong answer. There are few centres nearby, so I take pride in this job and keep an eye on what else is open.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AI Plateau sounds like the little shortcuts we already use, such as drafting a reply before an agent checks it. I wouldn’t announce a big change to the team over that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d feel mostly safe in the job, but not in my budget. My pay is low for leading a team, and one empty month of work would swallow what I’ve saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep doing calls and handovers in 2026, using the draft tool only after I check it against the account. During the first year of this small change, I’d set a weekly transfer into savings and keep a list of errors in drafted replies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about money, fairly calm about the work itself. A few saved minutes won’t pay my rent if the rota shrinks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What error has the draft tool made?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The draft tool once gave a customer a refund date that was not in the account. I caught it before sending, and I wrote the error in our handover book so the next agent would look twice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much could you save without missing a bill?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d start with the amount I spend on two coffees a week. That is small, but it is an amount I can leave alone without falling short on electricity.

say: I’d call **draft replies** a small aid after an agent checks them.
I’d tell colleagues our **handover work** still matters.
think: I think my **job** seems fairly safe under small changes.
I fear my **thin savings** would not cover missed pay.
I need **steady hours** because rent and electricity leave little slack.
do: Keep checking **draft replies** against accounts in 2026.
Transfer **coffee money** weekly into savings during the first year.
feel: **Uneasy** about money, calmer about daily work.
S0.quote: A few saved minutes won’t pay my rent if the rota shrinks.
fieldNote: Existing **budget pressure** raises her mood beyond simple work security.
She already records **tool errors** for colleagues.
Her **handover book** turns a single draft error into a warning for the next agent.

steps.text: Keep checking drafted customer replies against account records
Transfer the cost of two weekly coffees into emergency savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the team Steady Disruption means our routine answers may move to software before our difficult cases do. I’d ask management to publish error rates and what happens to agents whose chat volume falls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think they’ll keep the strongest agents and quietly stop replacing others. I’m strong at billing cases, but lower pay and almost no savings make even fewer hours a real problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d ask to join the monthly quality checks and learn the tool our agents already use now and then. In the first year routine chats move to AI, I’d apply for a paid quality-review slot and ask for enough hours on the rota to keep the rent covered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, though I can see a route to try. Being useful at checking mistakes is only protection if there is a paid job to do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What evidence would you bring to management?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would show the manager three billing replies that needed correction, with the account numbers hidden. A case that cost a customer money will say more than an argument about the future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take the review job at fewer hours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the quality slot paid less or had fewer hours, I’d stay on calls while looking elsewhere. I have few nearby options, so I cannot trade a real wage for a promising title.

say: I’d ask for **error rates** on automated answers.
I’d ask what happens to agents when **chat volume** falls.
think: I expect **fewer replacements** before open layoffs.
I would need **enough hours and pay** for a quality role to cover rent.
do: Join **monthly quality checks** and learn the existing tool in 2026.
Apply for a **review slot**; stay on calls if its pay or hours cannot cover rent.
feel: **Anxious**, with a possible route through checking errors.
S1.quote: Being useful at checking mistakes is only protection if there is a paid job to do it.
fieldNote: She uses **customer errors** as evidence rather than vague claims.
Her **pay threshold** limits which new roles she can accept.
She would **stay on calls** if a review title reduced her paid hours.

steps.text: Learn the centre’s existing reply tool during monthly quality checks
Take quality-review work only if hours and pay cover rent; otherwise stay on calls

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2028 makes this a staffing question now, not a distant technology story. I’d ask who can see why the system gave a customer a wrong bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think nearly all my calls and case notes could be handled by a cheaper system in 2028. The robots around 2031 do not matter much to my headset job, and there are few other centres close to home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I’d ask for a written trial on quality review and put any overtime pay straight into an emergency account. In the first year after 2028, I’d take a paid reviewer post if one survives; otherwise I’d apply outside the contact-centre field and cut subscriptions while I search.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be alarmed. Two years is short when I’m starting with less than one month saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the review trial need to include?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not wait until the system arrives to test the review work. I’d ask my supervisor for four paid shifts beside the quality team and a written account of what the job pays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would you look if review posts vanished?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If those posts vanish too, I’d apply for front-desk or service desk work where someone still has to handle a person in front of them. I know robots may reach hands-on tasks around 2031, so I would not call that a permanent refuge.

say: I’d ask for a **staffing plan** before 2028.
I’d demand access to the **reason** behind a wrong automated bill.
think: I think AGI could take my **calls and case notes** quickly.
I get little protection from the later **robot date** because I work at a desk.
do: Request a **paid review trial** and save overtime pay in 2026.
Seek paid review or **front-desk work** after 2028, cutting subscriptions while searching.
feel: **Alarmed** by the short runway and thin cushion.
S2.quote: Two years is short when I’m starting with less than one month saved.
fieldNote: She recognizes **2028** as the relevant exposure date.
Her fallback to **front-desk work** is temporary, not a claim of safety.
She asks for **four paid shifts** to test quality review before AGI arrives.

steps.text: Put overtime pay into an emergency account from 2026
Apply for paid quality-review or front-desk posts after 2028
Cancel subscriptions during the first year after AGI if searching for work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2031 gives us a few years to see whether quality review is a real career or just a temporary patch. I’d ask for a staffing plan with dates and wages, not only a training poster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With five years I could finish a part-time certificate in service operations and test other employers, though I’m not sure which jobs AGI will leave. I’d still expect the centre to need fewer people when it can reason through cases.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d ask which certificate the quality team actually values and start saving one pay day at a time. In the first year after 2031, I’d apply for a paid service operations or quality post and take interviews in nearby towns before giving up my flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but five years lets me make a measured move. I can learn one new system at a time when someone has shown it works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you choose a course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask two quality reviewers how many cases they really handle and what they are paid. Then I’d choose a certificate only if an employer counts it for an actual post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move to a town with more jobs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would travel for interviews before moving. A different town means deposits and transport costs, and I cannot spend my small cushion on a maybe.

say: I’d request a **dated staffing plan** with wages.
I’d tell colleagues **quality review** needs testing before we trust it.
think: I think five years may let me earn a **service operations certificate**.
I still expect the centre to need **fewer agents** after 2031.
do: Check **certificate value** with reviewers and save from each pay in 2026.
Interview for **paid operations roles** after 2031 before considering a move.
feel: **Anxious**, but able to move in measured stages.
S3.quote: A different town means deposits and transport costs, and I cannot spend my small cushion on a maybe.
fieldNote: She tests **course value** against actual vacancies.
She limits the **cost of moving** by interviewing first.
The **flat deposit** keeps her from moving for a job she has not secured.

steps.text: Take a service operations certificate only if an employer counts it for a posted role
Save a small amount after each pay day from 2026
Interview for paid service operations or quality posts after 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2036 gives us time to change the training plan instead of running one rushed course. I’d want the centre to show each year which tasks still need an agent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 37 by then, perhaps with different home costs, but ten years lets me build a cushion. I might be managing cases or quality by then; I know AGI can do thinking work too, so that would be a bridge, not a guarantee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d set a small automatic saving transfer and ask for one paid quality shift each month. If the centre offers those shifts, I’d take them to learn the work. In the first year after 2036, I’d compare my pay and duties with the AI-run service and move to a staffed customer-facing or operations role if my hours begin to fall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, though less frightened. A decade gives me room to change direction without pretending the final change disappears.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you test first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One quality shift a month would show me whether I like the work and whether the company pays people to do it. I could keep my calls while I find out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would stop you moving for a new role?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my flat until a new contract is signed. I can take a train to an interview; I cannot pay two deposits just to chase a possibility.

say: I’d ask for a **yearly task plan** through 2036.
I’d say training should follow **paid roles** as work changes.
think: I think ten years lets me build a **cushion**.
I see a quality title as a **bridge**, not protection from all thinking AI.
do: Set **automatic savings** and take monthly paid quality shifts if offered from 2026.
Seek **staffed operations work** after 2036 if hours fall.
S4.quote: A decade gives me room to change direction without pretending the final change disappears.
fieldNote: She uses a **monthly trial** to test work before committing.
She will **move jobs** only with a signed contract.
She would **keep her flat** while she interviews for a signed job offer.

steps.text: Set a small automatic transfer to savings after each payday
Take one paid quality-review shift each month if the centre offers it
Apply for staffed customer service or operations work if hours fall after 2036

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. The calls and case notes are thinking work, so the 2031 robot date would not save my place. A paid trial in quality review, an honest timetable for staff changes, and enough notice to move would actually help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You asked what I’d do, but the useful question is what the company will let agents see. If the software makes mistakes and we can’t see the reasons, even a human reviewer cannot fix much.

headlineQuote: If the software makes mistakes and we can’t see the reasons, even a human reviewer cannot fix much.
portrait: At **27**, Lena leads customer calls and chats and handles difficult billing cases.
She has a **college diploma**, lower pay and less than one month of expenses saved.
She uses AI **occasionally** and tests tools once colleagues have shown they work.
She seeks **quality review** work as routine answers and later reasoning tasks move to AI.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could replace her calls and case notes before she has savings or a new role.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid quality-review trial**, honest staffing timetable and clear notice would give her room to move.
